text: Implement a last-in, first-out stack using only queue operations: push to the back, pop or peek from the front, size, and empty. Support push, pop, top, and empty. Follow-up: can you use a single queue?

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. So I may only touch the queue through those operations, no indexing into the middle. The tension is that a queue is first in, first out, but a stack needs the newest element out first. So I need the newest element to sit at the queue's front. On push x, I add x to the back, then rotate the old elements around behind it, so x ends up at the front. Then pop and top just read the front, in constant time. And a single queue is enough, which answers the follow-up. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds reasonable. So where does the linear cost go?

Into push. It rotates size elements. First-in-first-out and last-in-first-out have opposite orders, so one operation must pay linear time to flip it. It can't be avoided, only placed. I'm making it push-heavy so pop and top, especially the read-only top, stay constant time.

This problem reminds me of an invariant-maintenance pattern: keep the container in the order the reads want, and pay to restore it on every write. Here the invariant is that front to back runs newest to oldest. Each push restores it by rotating the previous size elements behind the new one. Pop and top read the front, and empty just asks the queue.

Here's the plan. One: in push, record the size before pushing x. Two: push x to the back. Three: rotate that many times — push the front to the back, then pop the front. One thing worth flagging — the size must be recorded before the push. Rotating size plus one times would carry x to the back too, and the order would be wrong.

Alright, let me code this up. It's one queue. Push saves the old size, adds x, and rotates the old elements behind it, so x is now the front. Pop reads the front and removes it; top just returns the front; empty asks the queue. The line to get right is the size line at the top of push — it has to come before the push of x. A two-queue version does the same thing with a scratch queue: push x into it, pour the old queue in behind it, then swap the two.

Let's dry-run the code. Push one, two, three, then pop — expected three. The row that matters is push three: the queue is two, one, three goes to the back, and two rotations bring it to three, two, one. The queue is always the reverse of insertion order, so the front is the top. Pop removes three and leaves two, one. Proper last-in, first-out. That matches.
Could you make push constant time instead?

Yes, the pop-heavy version. Push goes straight to the back in constant time. On pop, I rotate the front size minus one elements to the back so the newest lands at the front, then remove it, which is linear. Top either does the same rotation and sends the element to the back again, or reads a cached last-pushed value. I'd pick based on which operation dominates: many pushes, go pop-heavy; many reads, go push-heavy.

Let me think about complexity here. Push is linear, since it rotates size elements. Pop, top, and empty are constant. Space is linear for one queue. The mirror problem, a queue built from two stacks, does better: with a lazy transfer each element moves at most once, so every operation is amortized constant time, even though a single pop can still be linear.
Clean. The rotate trick, the size-before-push detail, and the push-heavy versus pop-heavy tradeoff. Done.
